label: theorem:rational_uniformization
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{theorem:rational_uniformization}
    Let $f$ be a geometrically finite rational map whose Julia set is not homeomorphic to $\mathbb S^1$ or $\mathbb S^2$. There exists a quasiconformal map $g\colon \widehat \mathbb{C}\to \widehat \mathbb{C}$ that maps each Fatou component of $f$ onto a disk if and only if
    \begin{enumerate}[label=\normalfont(\arabic*)]
        \item\label{r:jordan} each Fatou component is a Jordan region,
        \item\label{r:parabolic3} all parabolic points have multiplicity $3$,
        \item\label{r:parabolic_basins} parabolic points do not lie on boundaries of periodic Fatou components other than their immediate basins, and
        \item\label{r:parabolic_tangent} for every pair of distinct Fatou components $U,V$ with $\overline{U}\cap \overline{V}\neq \emptyset$  the intersection $\overline{U}\cap \overline{V}$ consists of a single point $a_0$ that is not critical and is eventually mapped to a parabolic periodic cycle.
    \end{enumerate}
    Moreover, in this case the map $g|_{J(f)}$ is unique up to post-composition with conformal automorphisms of $\widehat\mathbb{C}$.

label: lemma:koebe_qm
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:koebe_qm}
    Let $U\subset \widehat\mathbb{C}$ be a connected open set, $E\subset U$ be a compact set and $f\colon U\to \widehat \mathbb{C}$ be a conformal embedding. Then $f\colon (E,\chi)\to (f(E),\chi)$ is $\eta$-quasi-M\"obius for a distortion function $\eta$ depending only on $U$ and $E$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $U=\widehat \mathbb{C}$, then $f$ is a M\"obius transformation, so it is $\eta$-quasi-M\"obius with $\eta(t)=t$. Suppose that $\widehat \mathbb{C}\setminus U\neq \emptyset$, so $\widehat \mathbb{C}\setminus f(U)\neq \emptyset$. Consider M\"obius transformations $\phi,\psi$ such that $\phi(U)\subset \mathbb{C}$ and $\psi(f(U))\subset \mathbb{C}$, and let $g=\psi \circ f\circ \phi^{-1}\colon \phi(U)\to \psi(f(U))$. By covering $\phi(E)$ with finitely many balls in $\phi(U)$ and applying Koebe's distortion theorem to each of them, we see that there exists a constant $M>0$ depending on $g$ and a constant $L\geq 1$ that depends only on $\phi(E)$ and $\phi(U)$ such that 
    $$L^{-1}M|z-w|\leq |g(z)-g(w)|\leq LM |z-w|\,\,\, \text{for all $z,w\in \phi(E)$}.$$
    Thus, $g\colon (\phi(E),|\cdot|)\to (\psi(f(E)), |\cdot|)$ is uniformly quasi-M\"obius, depending only on $U$ and $E$. The identity map from the Euclidean to the chordal metric preserves cross ratios, so $g\colon (\phi(E),\chi)\to (\psi(f(E)), \chi)$ is uniformly quasi-M\"obius, depending only on $U$ and $E$. Finally, since $\phi,\psi$ are M\"obius transformations, the map $f\colon (E,\chi)\to (f(E),\chi)$ is uniformly quasi-M\"obius depending only on $U$ and $E$, as desired.

label: lemma:tangent_local
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:tangent_local}
    Let $U_i,V_i\subset \widehat \mathbb{C}$ be quasidisks such that $\overline{U_i}\cap \overline{V_i}=\{z_i\}$ for $i=1,2$. Suppose that there exists a neighborhood $W_i$ of $z_i$ for $i=1,2$ and a quasiconformal map $\phi\colon W_1\to W_2$ such that $\phi(W_1\cap U_1)=W_2\cap U_2$ and $\phi(W_1\cap V_1)=W_2\cap V_2$. Then the pair $U_1,V_1$ is quasiconformally circularizable if and only if the pair $U_2,V_2$ is quasiconformally circularizable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, we extend $\phi$ to $\widehat \mathbb{C}$ as follows. By composing $\phi$ with isometries of $\mathbb{C}$ we assume that $z_1,z_2\in \mathbb{C}$. By shrinking $W_1$, we may assume that $W_1$ is a disk centered at $z_1$ and $\phi$ is a quasiconformal map from a neighborhood of $\overline{W_1}$ into $\mathbb{C}$. By Theorem \ref{q:qc_qs}, $\phi$ is quasisymmetric in $\overline{W_1}$. Thus, $\phi(\partial W_1)$ is a quasicircle (see \cite{Pommerenke:conformal}*{Proposition 5.10}) and $W_2\coloneqq \phi(W_1)$ is a quasidisk by Theorem \ref{theorem:quasidisk_quasicircle}. By Proposition \ref{proposition:quasidisk_extension}, $\phi|_{W_1}$ extends to a quasiconformal map of $\widehat \mathbb{C}$. We denote the extension by $\phi$ for simplicity.

    Without loss of generality, suppose that the pair $U_2,V_2$ is quasiconformally circularizable. Thus, there exists a quasiconformal map $\psi$ of $\widehat \mathbb{C}$ such that $\psi(U_2),\psi(V_2)$ are half-planes that are tangent at $\psi(z_2)=\infty$. Let $g=\psi\circ \phi$. Then $g(\partial U_1)$ and $g(\partial V_1)$ are Jordan curves in $\widehat \mathbb{C}$ that are straight lines in a neighborhood of $\infty$. It is elementary to find a chord-arc curve $J\subset \widehat \mathbb{C}\setminus (g(\overline{U_1})\cup g(\overline{V_1}))$ that is a straight line in a neighborhood of $\infty$ and otherwise it is smooth; see Figure \ref{figure:tangent_local}. By compactness, there exists a constant $K\geq 1$ such that $N_{1/K}(J)\subset \widehat \mathbb{C}\setminus (g(\overline{U_1})\cup g(\overline{V_1}))\subset N_K(J)$. Thus, the conclusion of Lemma \ref{lemma:chordarc} is true. By Theorem \ref{theorem:tangent} we conclude that the pair $g(U_1),g(V_1)$ is quasiconformally circularizable. Equivalently, the pair $U_1,V_1$ is quasiconformally circularizable.

label: lemma:repelling_invariant
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:repelling_invariant}
    Let $K_1,K_2\subset \widehat \mathbb{C}$ be Jordan curves such that $K_1\cap K_2=\{0\}$. Let $f$ be a repelling hyperbolic germ at $0$ such that each of $K_1,K_2$ is locally invariant under $f$ near $0$. Then no quasiconformal map of $\widehat \mathbb{C}$ can map $K_1$ and $K_2$ onto two circles.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By the Koenigs linearization theorem \cite{Milnor:dynamics}*{Theorem 8.2} we can conformally conjugate $f$ near $0$ to the map $g(z)=\lambda z$, where $\lambda=f'(0)$, so $|\lambda|> 1$. The Jordan curves $K_1,K_2$ contain Jordan arcs having $0$ as an interior point that correspond under the conjugating map to some Jordan arcs $J_1,J_2$. The arcs $J_1,J_2$ are locally invariant under $g$ in the sense that there exists a ball $B(0,r)$ such that $g(J_i\cap B(0,r))\subset J_i$ for $i=1,2$. If there exists a quasiconformal map of $\widehat \mathbb{C}$ mapping $K_1,K_2$ to circles, then $K_1,K_2$ would be quasicircles, so $J_1,J_2$ would be quasiarcs by the analyticity of the Koenigs linearizing map. The quasiarcs $J_1,J_2$ can be extended to quasicircles by Theorem \ref{theorem:rickman}. Thus, by Lemma \ref{lemma:tangent_local} it suffices to show that no quasiconformal map of $\widehat \mathbb{C}$ maps $J_1$ and $J_2$ onto two circular arcs. 

Suppose that there exists a quasiconformal map $\phi$ of $\widehat \mathbb{C}$ such that $\phi(0)=0$, $\phi(J_1)\subset \mathbb{R}$, and $\phi(J_2)$ is an arc of a circle $|z-Ri|=R$ in the upper half-plane that is tangent to the real line at $0$. By Theorem \ref{q:qc_qs}, if $r$ is chosen to be sufficiently small so that $\phi^{-1}(\infty)\notin \overline{B}(0,r)$, then $\phi$ is $\eta$-quasisymmetric in $B(0,r)$ for some distortion function $\eta$. Let $w_1=x\in \phi(J_1)\cap (0,R)$ and $w_2=x+iy\in \phi(J_2)$ so that $y=R-\sqrt{R^2-x^2}= \frac{x^2}{2R}+O(x^4)$ as $x\to 0^+$. Note that for small $x$ we have $w_1,w_2\in \phi(B(0,r))$,
\begin{align*}
    1\leq \frac{|w_2|}{|w_1|} \leq \sqrt{2}\quad \text{and}\quad \frac{|w_1-w_2|}{|w_1|}= \frac{x}{2R}+O(x^3).
\end{align*}
Let $z_i=\phi^{-1}(w_i)\in J_i\cap B(0,r)$, $i=1,2$. Since $\phi$ is $\eta$-quasisymmetric and $\phi(0)=0$, we have 
\begin{align}\label{lemma:repelling_invariant:1}
     \eta^{-1}(1)\leq \frac{|z_2|}{|z_1|}\leq 1/\eta^{-1}(1/\sqrt{2})\quad \text{and} \quad \frac{|z_1-z_2|}{|z_1|}=o(1)\quad \text{as $x\to 0$}.
\end{align}
By the first inequalities, there exists $c_0\geq 1$ that depends only on $\lambda$ and $\eta$ such that for some $n\in \mathbb{N}\cup \{0\}$ we have
$$ \frac{r}{c_0}\leq |\lambda^nz_i|<r \quad \text{for $i=1,2$}.$$
Note that the point $z_i'=\lambda^nz_i$ lies in $J_i'\coloneqq \{z\in J_i: r/c_0\leq |z|< r\}$ for $i=1,2$. Since the sets $J_1',J_2'$ have disjoint closures, we have $|z_1'-z_2'|\geq d_0$ for some constant $d_0>0$ independent of $z_1,z_2$. This implies that 
$$\frac{|z_1-z_2|}{|z_1|} \geq \frac{d_0}{r}.$$
This contradicts \eqref{lemma:repelling_invariant:1} as $x\to 0^+$.

label: lemma:preserve_parabolic
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:preserve_parabolic}
    Let $f$ be a rational map, $0$ be a parabolic fixed point of $f$ with $f'(0)=1$, and $U$ be a Jordan region that is an immediate basin of $0$ corresponding to an attraction vector $v$. Then there exist arbitrarily small repelling petals $P_1,P_2$ corresponding to repulsion vectors that are adjacent to $v$ and there exist non-overlapping Jordan arcs $E_{i}\subset \partial U\cap (P_i\cup \{0\})$ such that $g(E_i)\subset E_i$ for $i=1,2$, where $g$ is the local branch of $f^{-1}$ that fixes $0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Note that $U$ is a Fatou component and $\partial U$ is contained in the Julia set \cite{Milnor:dynamics}*{Lemma 10.5}. Thus, $\partial U$ cannot intersect any petal corresponding to an attraction vector for $0$. By the parabolic flower theorem \cite{Milnor:dynamics}*{Theorem 10.7}, there exist arbitrarily small petals corresponding to the attraction and repulsion vectors of $f$ whose union, together with $0$, gives a neighborhood of $0$. Also, these petals are Jordan regions cyclically ordered and each attracting petal intersects exactly two repelling petals, except in the case that the parabolic multiplicity is $2$, where there exist only two petals, an attracting one and a repelling one. Since $U$ cannot intersect any attracting petal other than the one corresponding to $v$, we conclude that $\partial U$ contains two non-overlapping arcs $E_1,E_2$ contained in repelling petals $P_1,P_2$, respectively, which correspond to vectors adjacent to $v$. Moreover, since $f(\partial U)=\partial U$, if $g$ is the local branch of $f^{-1}$ that fixes $0$, then $g$ maps each arc $E\subset \partial U$ near $0$ onto an arc $g(E)\subset \partial U$.
    
    If the multiplicity of $0$ is not $2$, then $P_1,P_2$ are disjoint attracting petals of $g$. For $i\in \{1,2\}$, each point of $E_i$ converges to $0$ under iteration of $g$ within the petal $P_i$. Note that $g(E_i)$ is an arc in $\partial U\cap (P_i\cup \{0\})$ with an endpoint at $0$ and either it contains $E_i$ or it is contained in $E_i$. If $g(E_i)\supsetneq E_i$ then the endpoint $z_0$ of $E_i$ that is different from $0$ satisfies $g^{\circ k}(z_0) \in (\partial U\cap P_i)\setminus E_i$ for each $k\in \mathbb{N}$. However, $E_i$ is a neighborhood of $0$ in $\partial U\cap P_i$, so $\lim_{k\to\infty}g^{\circ k}(z_0)\neq 0$, a contradiction. We conclude that $g(E_i)\subset E_i$, as desired. 

    Next, suppose that the multiplicity of $0$ is $2$. Then $P_1=P_2\eqqcolon P$. By shrinking $P$ if necessary, we assume that $g$ is injective in $\overline{P}$ and $\partial U\setminus  \overline{P}\neq \emptyset$, so $\partial U \cap  P$ has at least two components $A_i\supset E_i\setminus \{0\}$, $i=1,2$. Note that $A_i$ is an arc in $\partial U \cap P$ with an endpoint at $0$ and another endpoint $a_i\in \partial P$. Hence, $g(A_1)\subset A_1$ and $g(A_2)\subset A_2$ or $g(A_1)\subset A_2$ and $g(A_2)\subset A_1$. The map $g\colon \overline{P}\to g(\overline{P})$ induces a bijection between the set $\{0,a_1,a_2\}\subset \partial P$ and $\{0,g(a_1),g(a_2)\}\subset g(\partial P)$. Since $g$ is orientation-preserving, it preserves the cyclic order of the points $0,a_1,a_2$. From this it follows that $g(a_1)\in \overline{A_1}$ and $g(a_2)\in \overline{A_2}$. Therefore, $g(A_1)\subset A_1$ and $g(A_2)\subset A_2$. Arguing as in the previous paragraph, for $i=1,2$ we see that $g(E_i)\subset E_i$, otherwise, the endpoint of $E_i$ that is different from $0$ would not converge to $0$ under iteration of $g$.

label: lemma:arc_invariant_general
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:arc_invariant_general}
    Let $E$ be a Jordan arc with an endpoint at $0$ and $f$ be a homeomorphism from $E$ onto a subarc $f(E)$ of $E$ such that $0$ is the unique fixed point of $f$. Then $\bigcap_{k=0}^\infty f^{\circ k}(E)=\{0\}$. If, in addition, $f$ is a parabolic germ at $0$, then there exists an attraction vector $v$ for $f$ such that for any attracting petal $P$ for the direction $v$ we have $f^{\circ k}(E)\subset P\cup \{0\}$ for all sufficiently large $k\in \mathbb{N}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For the first part, by conjugating $f$ with a homeomorphism between $E$ and $[0,1]$, we may suppose that $E=[0,1]$, $f(E)=[0,a_1]$ for some $a_1\in (0,1)$ and $f\colon [0,1]\to [0,a_1]$ is an increasing homeomorphism having $0$ as the unique fixed point. Let $a_0=1$ and $a_k=f(a_{k-1})$, $k\in \mathbb{N}$. Then $a_{k+1}<a_{k}$ and $f^{\circ k}([0,1])=[0,a_k]$ for $k\in \mathbb{N}\cup \{0\}$. Thus, $\{a_k\}_{k\in \mathbb{N}}$ converges to a point of $[0,1]$ that is necessarily a fixed point of $f$. By assumption $0$ is the only such point. Thus, $\bigcap_{k=0}^\infty f^{\circ k}([0,1])=\{0\}$, as desired.

    Next, suppose that $f$ is a parabolic germ at $0$. By the first part, each point of $E$ is attracted to $0$ under iteration of $f$. By \cite{Milnor:dynamics}*{Lemma 10.1}, each point of $E$ has a neighborhood that is attracted to $0$ along one of the attracting directions of $f$. By the connectedness of $E$, all points of $E$ are attracted along the same attraction vector $v$. Let $P$ be an arbitrary attracting petal in the direction of $v$. Let $0,z_0$ be the endpoints of $E$. For $k\in \mathbb{N}$, let $z_k=f^{\circ k}(z_0)$ and $E(k)$ be the arc of $E$ from $z_{k-1}$ to $z_k$. Note that $f(E_k)=E_{k+1}$ for $k\in \mathbb{N}$. By the above, there exists $N\in \mathbb{N}$ such that $E(k)\subset P$ for $k\geq N$. Since $E=\bigcup_{k=1}^\infty E(k)\cup\{0\}$, it follows that $f^{\circ k}(E)\subset P\cup \{0\}$ for $k\geq N$.

label: lemma:germ_tangent_reduction
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:germ_tangent_reduction}
    Let $f,K_1,K_2$ be as in the assumptions of Theorem \ref{theorem:germ_tangent_modification}. Then there exists a quasiconformal map $\psi\colon \widehat \mathbb{C}\to \widehat \mathbb{C}$ and a parabolic germ $g$ at $0$ such that $\psi(K_1)=\mathbb{R}\cup \{\infty\}$ and $g,\psi(K_1),\psi(K_2)$ satisfy the assumptions of Theorem \ref{theorem:germ_tangent_modification}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By replacing $f$ with $f^{-1}$, we may suppose that $P_1$ is an attracting petal corresponding to an attracting vector $v_1$. For $i=1,2$ consider a Jordan arc $E_{i1}\subset K_i\cap (P_1\cup \{0\})$ with an endpoint at $0$ such that $f(E_{i1})\subset f(E_{i1})$. Since $f$ is a homeomorphism in $P_1$ and each point of $P_1$ is attracted to $0$ under iteration, we conclude that for each $z\in E_{i1}\setminus \{0\}$ the point $f(z)$ lies in the open subarc of $E_{i1}$ from $0$ to $z$.
    
    Let $D$ be the Jordan region whose boundary is $K_1$ and $K_2\subset \overline{D}$. By Theorem \ref{theorem:quasidisk_quasicircle}, $D$ is a quasidisk. By Proposition \ref{proposition:quasidisk_extension} there exists a quasiconformal map $\psi$ of $\widehat \mathbb{C}$ such that $\psi(K_1)=\mathbb{R}\cup \{\infty\}$, $\psi(0)=0$, $\psi(D)=\mathbb H$, and $\psi|_D$ is conformal. Here $\mathbb H$ denotes the upper half-plane. We conjugate $f$ with $\psi$ to obtain a holomorphic map $g$ in a neighborhood of $0$ in $\mathbb H$. Note that $g$ extends continuously to the real line near $0$ and maps it into itself. Thus, by Schwarz reflection we may extend $g$ to a holomorphic map in a neighborhood of $0$ that fixes $0$.

    Without loss of generality, suppose that $E_{11}$ is mapped under $\psi$ to an interval $(0,s_0)$. By the behavior of $f$ in $E_{11}$, we conclude that $0<g(x)<x$ for each $x\in(0,s_0)$. This implies that $0\leq g'(0)\leq 1$.  Note that the petal $P_2$ for $f$ is either attracting or repelling. By assumption, for $i=1,2$ there exists an arc $E_{i2}\subset K_i\cap (P_2\cup \{0\})$ with properties analogous to those of $E_{i1}$ above. Let $(-t_0,0)=\psi(E_{12})$. We claim that $g$ is a parabolic germ at $0$. If $P_2$ is a repelling petal, then we have $g(x)<x$ for each $x\in (-t_0,0)$, which implies that $g'(0)\geq 1$. Thus, $g'(0)=1$. Clearly $g$ is not the identity map, so it is a parabolic germ at $0$. 
    
    Next, suppose that $P_2$ is an attracting petal. Fix $j\in \{1,2\}$. By Lemma \ref{lemma:arc_invariant_general}, if $S_j$ is an arbitrary sector at $0$ that contains $v_j$ then $f^{\circ k}(E_{ij})\subset S_j\cup \{0\}$ for all sufficiently large $k\in \mathbb{N}$ and for $i=1,2$. Thus, the arc $E_{ij}$ is asymptotic to the attracting vector $v_j$. Since $f$ is parabolic, there exists a repulsion vector $v$ that is between the attraction vectors $v_1,v_2$ and a repelling petal $P$ for the direction $v$ that is disjoint from small sectors $S_j$, $j=1,2$, as above. In particular, we may find a sufficiently small repelling petal $P$ as above that is contained in $D$. That is, each point of $P$ is attracted to $0$ under iteration of $f^{-1}$. This proves that there are points of $\mathbb H$ that are attracted to $0$ under iteration of $g^{-1}$. If $|g'(0)|<1$, then all points in a neighborhood of $0$ would be attracted to $0$ under iteration of $g$ by \cite{Milnor:dynamics}*{Lemma 8.1}, a contradiction. Thus, the only remaining case is that $g'(0)=1$. Hence, $g$ is again a parabolic germ.

    It remains to prove that the conditions of Theorem \ref{theorem:germ_tangent_modification} remain true for $g$. Let $F_{11}=(0,s_0)=\psi(E_{11})$ and $F_{21}=\psi(E_{21})$, which satisfy $g(F_{i1})\subset F_{i1}$ for $i=1,2$ by the dynamics of $f$. Clearly, each point of $F_{11}$ is attracted to $0$ in the direction of the positive real axis. We claim that the same is true for $F_{21}$. By the dynamics of $f$, each point of $F_{21}$ is attracted to $0$ under iteration of $g$. By Lemma \ref{lemma:arc_invariant_general} there exists an attraction vector $v\in \overline{\mathbb H}$ for $g$ such that $F_{21}$ is asymptotic to $v$. If $v$ is not in the direction of the positive real axis, then there exists a repulsion direction between the positive real axis and the vector $v$. In particular, there exists a repelling petal $Q$ for $g$ in $\mathbb H$ that lies between (in the sense of cyclic order) $F_{11}$ and $F_{21}$. This implies that there exists a repelling petal $\psi^{-1}(Q)$ for $f$ that is between $E_{11}$ and $E_{21}$. Note that $E_{11}$ and $E_{21}$ are asymptotic to $v_1$, in view of Lemma \ref{lemma:arc_invariant_general}. Thus, if $Q$ is sufficiently small, then $\psi^{-1}(Q)$ is necessarily contained in a small sector that contains $v_1$ and that does not contain repulsion vectors of $f$. So, points of $\psi^{-1}(Q)$ cannot be attracted to $0$ in the direction of a repulsion vector of $f$ under iteration of $f^{-1}$. This is a contradiction. Thus, the claim is proved. Now, if we consider any attracting petal $Q_1$ for $g$ for the direction of the positive real axis, then by replacing $F_{i1}$ with an iterate, in view of Lemma \ref{lemma:arc_invariant_general}, we may have $F_{i1}\subset Q_1\cup \{0\}$ for $i=1,2$. In the same way we argue for $F_{i2}=\psi(E_{i2})$, $i=1,2$.

label: lemma:lift
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:lift}
    Let $f_1,f_2$ be holomorphic germs at $0$ such that $f_1(z)=az^m+O(z^{m+1})$ and $f_2(z)=\lambda z+bz^{n+1}+O(z^{n+2})$ for some $a,\lambda \neq 0$ and $m,n\in \mathbb{N}$. 
    \begin{enumerate}[label=\normalfont(\arabic*)]
        \item\label{lemma:lift:existence} There exists a holomorphic germ $h$ at $0$ such that $f_2\circ f_1=f_1\circ h$ and $h'(0)^m=\lambda$. 
        \item\label{lemma:lift:choices} There are exactly $m$ choices for $h$, one for each local branch of $f_1^{-1}$ so that $h=f^{-1}_1\circ f_2\circ f_1$.
        \item\label{lemma:lift:1} If $\lambda=1$, then we may take
    $$h(z)=z+ c z^{nm+1}+O(z^{nm+2}) \quad \text{as $z\to 0$},$$
    where $c\neq 0$ if and only if $b\neq 0$.
    \end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The map $f_1$ is locally $m$-to-$1$ near $0$, so there exists a conformal map $\phi$ in a neighborhood of $0$ that fixes $0$ and satisfies $f_1(z)=\phi(z)^m$. Next, we have
    $$f_2(z^m)= \lambda z^m+ bz^{m(n+1)}+O(z^{m(n+2)})= \lambda z^m \left( 1+ \frac{b}{\lambda}z^{mn}+O(z^{m(n+1)})\right).$$
    Since this map is locally $m$-to-$1$ near $0$, there exists a conformal map $\widetilde h$ in a neighborhood  of $0$ that fixes $0$ and satisfies $f_2(z^m)= \widetilde h(z)^m$; there are $m$ choices of $\widetilde h$, differing by multiplication with an $m$-th root of unity and we fix one such map. Thus, 
    $$\widetilde h(z)=\mu z \left( 1+ \frac{b}{\lambda}z^{mn}+O(z^{m(n+1)})\right)^{1/m}= \mu z+\frac{\mu b}{m\lambda} z^{nm+1}+O(z^{nm+2})$$
    for a choice $\mu$ of the $m$-th root of $\lambda$. Finally, we set $h=\phi^{-1}\circ \widetilde h\circ \phi$, which satisfies $h'(0)=\mu$. Observe that $h$ satisfies the claimed identity $f_2\circ f_1=f_1\circ h$. This proves \ref{lemma:lift:existence}.

    If $z\mapsto z^{1/m}$ is a branch of the $m$-th root defined in an appropriate open set not containing $0$, then $f_1^{-1}(z)=\phi^{-1}(z^{1/m})$ is a branch of $f_1^{-1}$. Let $g=f_1^{-1}\circ f_2\circ f_1$ and $\widetilde g= \phi\circ g\circ \phi^{-1}$, defined in appropriate open sets. We have
    $$\widetilde g(z)^m= \phi( g(\phi^{-1}(z)))^m= f_1( g(\phi^{-1}(z)))= f_2( f_1(\phi^{-1}(z)))=f_2(z^m)= \widetilde h(z)^m.$$
    This implies that $\widetilde h$ differs from $\widetilde g$ by multiplication with an $m$-th root of unity. So, $\widetilde g$ and $g$ may be extended in a neighborhood of $0$. Thus, the chosen branch of $f_1^{-1}$ yields a map $g$ satisfying \ref{lemma:lift:existence}, as desired. 
    
    Next, suppose that $\lambda=\mu=1$. We have
    \begin{align*}
       \phi(z+\delta)-\phi(z)-\phi'(z)\delta&= \int_{[z,z+\delta]}(\phi'(\zeta) -\phi'(z))\, d\zeta\\ &= \int_{[z,z+\delta]} \int_{[z,\zeta]}\phi''(s)\, ds\, d\zeta =O(\delta^2).
    \end{align*}
    We expand $h(z)=z+ cz^{l}+O(z^{l+1})$, where $c\neq 0$. For $\delta=h(z)- z$ we have
    \begin{align*}
       \phi(h(z))= \phi( z+\delta) &= \phi( z)+\phi'( z)\delta+ O(\delta^2)\\
       &= \phi(z)+(\phi'(0)+O(z))(cz^l +O(z^{l+1}))+O(z^{2l}). 
    \end{align*}
    Moreover, 
    \begin{align*}
        \widetilde h(\phi(z))= \phi(z)+ \frac{b}{m} \phi(z)^{nm+1}+O(z^{nm+2}).
    \end{align*}
    Thus, 
    $$\frac{b}{m}\phi(z)^{nm+1}+O(z^{nm+2})= \phi'(0)c z^l+ O(z^{l+1}).$$
    If $b\neq 0$, it follows that $l=nm+1$ and $\frac{b}{m}\phi'(0)^{nm+1}=\phi'(0)c$. If $b=0$, then $l>nm+1$. This proves \ref{lemma:lift:1}.

label: lemma:no_infinite
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:no_infinite}
    Let $f$ be a geometrically finite rational map.
    \begin{enumerate}[label=\normalfont(\arabic*)]
        \item\label{lemma:no_infinite:0} If $U,V$ are distinct Fatou components such that $V$ is simply connected and fixed, and $a_0\in \overline{U}\cap \overline{V}$ is a fixed point, then $f(U)\neq V$. 
        \item\label{lemma:no_infinite:00} If $U,V$ are distinct Fatou components such that $V,f(V)$ are Jordan regions and $a_0\in \overline{U}\cap \overline{V}$ is not a critical point, then $f(U)\neq f(V)$. 
        \item\label{lemma:no_infinite:1} If a periodic point lies in the boundary of a simply connected Fatou component $U$ of $f$, then $U$ is periodic. 
        \item\label{lemma:no_infinite:2} Each pre-periodic point lies in the boundaries of at most finitely many simply connected Fatou components.
    \end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cite{LeiYongcheng:local_connectivity}*{Lemma 2.1}, $\partial V$ is locally connected. By \cite{TanYin96long}*{Corollary 3.3}, the point $a_0$ has finitely many prime ends in $V$. In particular, there exist finitely many cross cuts bounding disjoint regions $Z_1,\dots,Z_k \subset U$ whose union is a neighborhood $Z$ of $a_0$ in $V$. Note that $a_0$ cannot be a critical point. So, by taking $Z$ sufficiently small, we assume that $f$ is injective in $Z$. This implies that the regions $f(Z_1),\dots,f(Z_k)$ are disjoint and are in correspondence with the prime ends of $a_0$; one can see this by conformally conjugating $f|_V$ to a Blaschke product in $\mathbb{D}$. Therefore, $f(Z)$ is a neighborhood of $a_0$ in $V$. Since $f$ is injective near $a_0$, no point of $U$ near $a_0$ can be mapped to a point of $f(Z)$. Since $f(Z)$ is a neighborhood of $a_0$ in $V$, no point of $U$ near $a_0$ can be mapped to a point of $V$. Thus  $f(U)\neq V$ and \ref{lemma:no_infinite:0} is true.

    Next, we prove \ref{lemma:no_infinite:00}. By the above argument, given that $a_0,f(a_0)$ correspond to a unique prime end in $V,f(V)$, respectively, we see that there exists a neighborhood $Z$ of $a_0$ in $V$ that is mapped to a neighborhood $f(Z)$ of $a_0$ in $f(V)$. Now we argue as above. Since $f$ is injective near $a_0$, no point of $U$ near $a_0$ can be mapped to a point of $V$ near $a_0$. Thus, $f(U)\neq f(V)$. 
    
    We prove \ref{lemma:no_infinite:1}. Suppose that $U$ is a strictly pre-periodic Fatou component and $a_0\in \partial U$ is a periodic point. By replacing $f$ with an iterate, suppose that $a_0$ is fixed and $V=f(U)$ is fixed. Since $f(\partial U)=\partial V$ and $\partial U$ is connected, the set $\partial V$ is connected, so $V$ is simply connected. However, this contradicts \ref{lemma:no_infinite:0}, so \ref{lemma:no_infinite:1} holds. Now we justify \ref{lemma:no_infinite:2}. By part \ref{lemma:no_infinite:1} and the finiteness of periodic Fatou components, each periodic point lies in the boundary of at most finitely many simply connected Fatou components. Thus, each pre-periodic point has the same property.

label: proposition:component_dependent
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{proposition:component_dependent}
    Let $f$ be a geometrically finite rational map and $U, V$ be Fatou components whose orbits $\{f^{\circ n}(U)\}_{n\geq 0}$, $\{f^{\circ n}(V)\}_{n\geq 0}$ consist of Jordan regions. Suppose that there exists an open set $W$ such that $W\cap \overline{U}\cap \overline{V}=\{a_0\}$ and the sets $\partial U\cap \overline{W}$ and $\partial V\cap \overline{W}$ are quasiarcs. Assume that one of the following alternatives holds.
    \begin{enumerate}[label=\normalfont(\arabic*)]
        \item\label{proposition:component_dependent:1} $a_0$ is mapped to a parabolic periodic cycle of multiplicity $3$ by an iterate of $f$ that is a local homeomorphism near $a_0$.
        \item\label{proposition:component_dependent:2} $a_0$ is mapped to a parabolic periodic cycle of multiplicity $2$ by an iterate of $f$ that is locally two-to-one at $a_0$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Then there exists a quasiconformal map $\phi$ of $\widehat \mathbb{C}$ that maps $\partial U\cap \overline{W}$ and $\partial V\cap \overline{W}$ onto two circular arcs that are tangent to each other.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $l$ be the pre-period of $a_0$ and let $p$ be a multiple of the period of $b_0=f^{\circ l}(a_0)$ so that $f^{\circ p}$ fixes the attracting directions at the parabolic point $b_0$, i.e., $(f^{\circ p})'(b_0)=1$. We apply Lemma \ref{lemma:lift} for the holomorphic germs $f_1=f^{\circ l}$ and $f_2=f^{\circ p}$ at $a_0$. In both alternative assumptions the map $f_1=f^{\circ l}$ is locally $m$-to-$1$ at $a_0$ and the map $f_2=f^{\circ p}$ has a parabolic fixed point at $b_0$ with multiplicity $n+1$ for some $n,m\in \mathbb{N}$. By Lemma \ref{lemma:lift} we obtain a parabolic germ $h$ at $a_0$ with multiplicity $nm+1$ such that $f_2\circ f_1=f_1\circ h$. Under assumption \ref{proposition:component_dependent:1}, we have $m=1$ and $n=2$, so the multiplicity of the parabolic point $a_0$ of $h$ is $3$. Under assumption \ref{proposition:component_dependent:2}, we have $m=2$ and $n=1$, so the multiplicity of the parabolic point $0$ of $h$ is again $3$.

    Under either assumption, we claim that $f_1(U)$ is an immediate basin of the parabolic point $b_0$. If not, then $f_1(U)$ is disjoint from all attracting petals at $b_0$. By Lemma \ref{lemma:avoid_petals}, any arc of  $f_1(\partial U)$ that contains $b_0$ in its interior is not a quasiarc and $\partial U\cap W$ is not a quasiarc, a contradiction. Similarly, $f_1(V)$ is an immediate basin of $b_0$.     
    
    Suppose \ref{proposition:component_dependent:1} holds. The map $f_1$ is a local homeomorphism near $a_0$ and we have $h=f_1^{-1}\circ f_2\circ f_1$, where $f_1^{-1}$ is a local inverse branch of $f_1$ that maps $b_0$ to $a_0$.  Given that $a_0$ is not a critical point of $f_1$, by Lemma \ref{lemma:no_infinite} \ref{lemma:no_infinite:00} the sets $f_1(U)$ and $f_1(V)$ are distinct Fatou components each contained in one of the two parabolic basins of the map $f_2$ for the point $b_0$. By Lemma \ref{lemma:preserve_parabolic} each of the boundaries $f_1(\partial U)$ and $f_1(\partial V)$ contains two non-overlapping arcs with a common endpoint at $b_0$, contained in opposite repelling petals of $f_2$, and each of these arcs is mapped into itself under a branch of $f_2^{-1}$. It follows that each of $\partial U,\partial V$ contains two non-overlapping arcs with a common endpoint at $a_0$ contained in opposite repelling petals of $h$, and each of these arcs is mapped into itself under $h^{-1}$. By Theorem \ref{theorem:rickman}, we can extend the quasiarcs $\partial U\cap \overline{W}$ and $\partial V\cap \overline{W}$ to quasicircles $K_1,K_2$ as in Theorem \ref{theorem:germ_tangent_modification}. Therefore, by Theorem~\ref{theorem:germ_tangent_modification}, there exists a quasiconformal map of $\widehat \mathbb{C}$ that maps $\partial U\cap \overline{W}$ and $\partial V\cap \overline{W}$ onto two circular arcs, as desired. 

    Next, we assume that \ref{proposition:component_dependent:2} holds. Then $f_1$ is locally $2$-to-$1$ at $a_0$. Consider a small repelling petal $P$ of $f_2$ at $b_0$ that is a Jordan region. By Lemma \ref{lemma:preserve_parabolic}, $f_1(\partial U)\cap P$ contains two non-overlapping arcs with an endpoint at $b_0$ and each of these arcs is mapped into itself under a branch of $f_2^{-1}$. The set $f_1^{-1}(P)$ has two components $P_1,P_2$, and in the closure of each of them $f_1$ topologically conjugates $h$ to $f_2$. Thus, $P_1,P_2$ are repelling petals of $h$. Moreover, each of $\partial U,\partial V$ contains two non-overlapping arcs with a common endpoint at $a_0$, contained in opposite repelling petals of $h$, and each of these arcs is mapped into itself under $h^{-1}$. Therefore, we are in the setting of Theorem \ref{theorem:germ_tangent_modification} as before.

label: prop:comparisonhyperbolicmetric
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:comparisonhyperbolicmetric}
    Let $V,Q \subset \mathbb{H}$ be Jordan regions such that $V\subset Q$ and the sets
    $$
    I = \partial V \cap \mathbb{R}  \,\,\,\text{and}\,\,\, J= \partial Q \cap \mathbb{R}
    $$
    are closed intervals so that $\operatorname{dist}(I,\mathbb{R}\setminus J)>0$. Assume that ${Q \setminus \overline{V}}$ is a quadrilateral, whose vertical sides are the closures of the two components of $J\setminus I$, and  $\operatorname{Mod} (Q\setminus \overline{V}) \geq K^{-1}$ for some $K\geq 1$. Then 
    $$\rho_{\mathbb H}(z)\leq \rho_Q(z)\leq C(K) \rho_{\mathbb H}(z)\,\,\, \text{for all $z\in V$.} $$
head: environment

label: prop:comparison:ineq
title: Proof
body_md:
The lower bound follows from the Schwarz lemma; see \cite{BeardonMinda:hyperbolic}*{Theorem 8.1}. To prove the upper bound, we use the estimate (see \cite{BeardonMinda:hyperbolic}*{Theorem 8.2})
    \begin{align}\label{prop:comparison:ineq}
        \rho_Q(z) \leq \frac{2}{\operatorname{dist}(z, \partial Q)}, \,\,\, z\in Q.
   \end{align}
    We write $\partial Q = J \cup \Gamma$, where $\Gamma = \overline{\partial Q \cap \mathbb{H}}$. Let  $Q'$  be the double of $Q$ along $J$ and $V'$ be the double of $V$ along $I$. Let $A = Q' \setminus \overline{V'}$, which is an annulus. Since $\operatorname{Mod} (Q\setminus \overline{V})\geq K^{-1}$, we have 
    $$\operatorname{Mod} A\geq (2K)^{-1}$$
    by the discussion in Section \ref{section:modulus}.  Let $z_0 \in V$ and $w_0 \in \partial Q'$ so that 
    $$|w_0 - z_0| = \operatorname{dist}(z_0, \partial  Q') = \operatorname{dist}(z_0, \Gamma).$$ 
    Note that $A$ separates $z_0, \overline{z_0}$ from $w_0, \infty$.
    By Teichm\"uller's module theorem \cite{LehtoVirtanen:quasiconformal}*{Section II.1.3}, there is an increasing function $\Psi\colon (0,\infty) \to (0,\infty)$ so that
    $$
    \frac{1}{2K}\leq \operatorname{Mod} A \leq \Psi\left(\frac{|w_0-z_0|}{|z_0-\overline{z_0}|}\right) = \Psi\left(\frac{\operatorname{dist}(z_0, \Gamma)}{2\operatorname{Im}(z_0)}\right).
    $$
    Therefore, there exists $\delta = \delta(K)\geq 1$ so that $\operatorname{dist}(z_0, \Gamma) \geq \delta^{-1}\operatorname{Im}(z_0)$. Also, note that $\operatorname{dist}(z_0,\partial Q)=\operatorname{dist}(z_0,\Gamma)$ or $\operatorname{dist}(z_0,\partial Q)=\operatorname{Im}(z_0)$. Thus, by \eqref{prop:comparison:ineq},
    $$
    \rho_Q(z_0) \leq \frac{2}{\operatorname{dist}(z_0, \partial Q)} \leq \frac{2\delta }{\operatorname{Im}(z_0)} = 2\delta \rho_{\mathbb{H}}(z_0).
    $$
    This proves the upper bound.

body_md:
\label{proposition:quasidisk_uniform}
    Let $f$ be a geometrically finite rational map and $U$ be a Fatou component whose forward orbit consists of Jordan regions. There exists a constant $L=L(f)\geq 1$ such that if $U$ is a quasidisk, then it is an $L$-quasidisk.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{lemma:no_infinite} \ref{lemma:no_infinite:2}, there are finitely many simply connected Fatou components $\Omega$ whose closures contain critical points. We choose $k_0\geq 1$ so that whenever a critical point of $f$ lies in the closure of a simply connected Fatou component $\Omega$, the pre-period $l_\Omega$ of $\Omega$ is at most $k_0$. There are finitely many Fatou components $U$ with $l_U< k_0$. Thus, if $U$ is a quasidisk, then it is an $L$-quasidisk for some uniform $L\geq 1$. 
    
    Next, we suppose that $l_U\geq k_0$. Let $V=f^{\circ m}(U)$ for $m=l_U-k_0\geq 0$, so $l_V=k_0$. By assumption, $V$ is a Jordan region. We will show that $U$ is a uniform quasidisk, depending only on $V$, but not on $m$. This is sufficient, since there are finitely many Fatou components $V$ with $l_V=k_0$. Since $V$ is not periodic, $\overline{V}$ does not contain any parabolic periodic points by Lemma \ref{lemma:no_infinite} \ref{lemma:no_infinite:1}. Thus, $\overline{V}$ is disjoint from the accumulation points of the post-critical set. By the choice of $k_0$, $\overline{V}$ has a positive distance from the post-critical set. Consider a  Jordan region $N\supset \overline{V}$ that is disjoint from the post-critical set of $f$. 
    
    The map $g=f^{\circ m}\colon U\to V$ is conformal since $V$ is simply connected and $g$ has no critical points.  Moreover,  $g^{-1}$ extends conformally to the neighborhood $N$ of $\overline{V}$. Since $U$ is a quasidisk, $\partial U$ is a quasicircle by Theorem \ref{theorem:quasidisk_quasicircle}. The fact that $g$ is a diffeomorphism implies that $\partial V$ also satisfies the Ahlfors condition and is a quasicircle. There are only finitely many Fatou components of pre-period $k_0$, so $\partial V$ is a uniform quasicircle. By Lemma \ref{lemma:koebe_qm}, the map $g^{-1}\colon (\partial  V, \chi)\to (\partial U, \chi)$ is uniformly quasi-M\"obius. Thus, $\partial U$ is a uniform quasicircle, being the quasi-M\"obius image of a quasicircle. Hence, $U$ is a uniform quasidisk.

label: lemma:lift:arcs_invariant
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:lift:arcs_invariant}
    Let $\phi(z)=z^d$, $d\geq 2$. Let $f,h$ be orientation-preserving homeomorphisms in neighborhoods of $\overline{\mathbb{D}}$ that fix $0$ such that $h$ is a lift of $f$ under $\phi$.
    \begin{enumerate}[label=\normalfont (\arabic*)]
        \item\label{lemma:lift:arc} Let $E\subset \mathbb{D}$ be a Jordan arc with an endpoint at $0$ and an endpoint at $\partial \mathbb{D}$ that is locally invariant near $0$ under $f$.
        \item Suppose that some lift $\widetilde E$ of $E$ is locally invariant near $0$ under $h$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Then every lift of $E$ is locally invariant near $0$ under $h$. The same conclusion holds for the lifts of any arc $F$ satisfying \ref{lemma:lift:arc} such that $E\cap F=\{0\}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The arc $E$ has $d$ preimages $E_1,\dots,E_d$ under $\phi$. Each $E_i$ is a Jordan arc with endpoints at $0$ and at some point $z_i \in  \partial \mathbb{D}$. The arcs are disjoint except at $0$, which is their common endpoint. We assume that the points $z_i\in \partial \mathbb{D}$, $i\in \{1,\dots,d\}$, have the counter-clockwise order. Note that $h$ acts transitively on these arcs in the sense that there exists a neighborhood $U$ of $0$ such that for each $i\in \{1,\dots,d\}$ there exists a unique $j\in \{1,\dots,d\}$ such that $h(E_j\cap U)\subset E_i$. Hence, $h$ induces a bijection $\tilde h\colon \mathbb{Z}_d\to \mathbb{Z}_d$ with the property that  $\tilde h(j)=i$ if $h(E_j\cap U)\subset E_i$. Since $h$ is an orientation-preserving homeomorphism, the map $\tilde h$ must be a translation. By assumption, a lift of $E$ is locally invariant under $h$ near $0$. This implies that $\tilde h$ has a fixed point, so it is the identity map. Thus, every lift of $E$ is locally invariant under $h$.  

    Next, consider an arc $F$ satisfying \ref{lemma:lift:arc} such that $E\cap F=\{0\}$. Then $F$ has $d$ lifts each of which is between two lifts of $E$ and $h$ acts transitively on the lifts of $F$. Since each lift of $E$ is locally invariant near $0$ under $h$, and $h$ is an orientation-preserving homeomorphism, we see that each lift of $F$ is also locally invariant near $0$ under $h$.

\label{lem:isolatedpre-periodic}

title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove the sufficiency. Suppose that $U_i$ is a quasidisk for each $i\in I$, as in \ref{theorem:uniformization_general:2}. By Theorem \ref{theorem:schottky}, it suffices to prove that for every pair of distinct $i,j$ there exists a uniformly quasiconformal homeomorphism of $\widehat \mathbb{C}$ that maps $U_i$ and $U_j$ to disks. If $\overline{U_i}\cap \overline{U_j}=\emptyset$, then the conclusion follows from Corollary \ref{corollary:separated_quasidisk}. Suppose that $\overline{U_i}\cap \overline{U_j}=\{a_0\}$. By the assumptions, combined with Proposition \ref{proposition:component_dependent} and Lemma \ref{lemma:tangent_local}, we see that the pair $U_i,U_j$ is quasiconformally circularizable. By Proposition \ref{proposition:circularizable_gf},  the pair $U_i, U_j$ is uniformly quasiconformally circularizable, as desired. The last uniqueness statement follows from the uniqueness part of Theorem \ref{theorem:schottky}.

We now prove the necessity. Suppose that there exists a quasiconformal map $g$ of $\widehat \mathbb{C}$ such that $g(U_i)$ is a disk for each $i\in I$, as in \ref{theorem:uniformization_general:1}. It is obviously necessary that $U_i$ is a quasidisk for each $i\in I$. Also, if $\overline{U_i}\cap \overline{U_j}\neq \emptyset$ for some $i\neq j$, then $\overline{U_i}\cap \overline{U_j}$ consists of a single point $a_0$, given that the Julia set is not a Jordan curve. 


By Lemma~\ref{lem:isolatedpre-periodic}, $a_0$ is pre-periodic. Let $b_0$ be a periodic point in the orbit of $a_0$. Observe that the point $b_0$ must be repelling or parabolic; indeed, there are no Cremer points for geometrically finite rational maps \cite{Milnor:dynamics}*{Theorem 11.17}.
Let $l$ be the pre-period of $a_0$ and $p$ be a multiple of the period of $b_0=f^{\circ l}(a_0)$ so that $f^{\circ p}$ fixes all simply connected Fatou components that contain $b_0$ in their boundary; there are finitely many such Fatou components by Lemma \ref{lemma:no_infinite} \ref{lemma:no_infinite:1}. Define $f_1=f^{\circ l}$, $f_2=f^{\circ p}$. By Lemma \ref{lemma:lift} there exists a parabolic germ $h$ at $a_0$ such that $f_2\circ f_1=f_1\circ h$. 


Suppose that $b_0$ is repelling for $f_2$, so by Lemma \ref{lemma:lift}, $a_0$ is repelling for $h$. Given that $f_1(U_i)$ and $f_1(U_j)$ are Jordan regions that are fixed under $f_2$, we see that $f_2$ locally preserves their boundaries near $b_0$. Suppose first that $f_1=f^{\circ l}$ is locally injective near $a_0$. Then we see directly that $h$ locally preserves $\partial U_i$ and $\partial U_j$ near $a_0$. Now, suppose that $f_1$ has a critical point at $a_0$. If $f_1^{-1}$ is a branch of the inverse of $f_1$ that maps a neighborhood of $b_0$ in $f_1(U_i)$ onto a neighborhood of $a_0$ in $U_i$, then we may choose $h$ so that $h=f_1^{-1}\circ f_2\circ f_1$; see Lemma \ref{lemma:lift} \ref{lemma:lift:choices}. Thus, we may have that $h$ locally preserves $\partial U_i$ near $a_0$. By Lemma \ref{lemma:lift:arcs_invariant}, $\partial U_j$ is also locally invariant under $h$ near $a_0$. In both cases, by applying Lemma \ref{lemma:repelling_invariant} we see that no quasiconformal map of the sphere can map $U_i$ and $U_j$ to two disks, a contradiction.


Therefore, $b_0$ is a parabolic point for $f_2$. Let $m\geq1$ be the local degree of $f_1$ at $a_0$ and $n+1\geq 2$ be the parabolic multiplicity of the point $b_0$ for the map $f_2$. Then the parabolic multiplicity of $a_0$ for the map $h$ is $nm+1$ by Lemma \ref{lemma:lift} \ref{lemma:lift:1}. We have $nm+1=2$ if and only if $f_1$ is locally injective near $a_0$ and the multiplicity of $b_0$ for the map $f_2$ is $2$. In this case, any Fatou component that contains $b_0$ in its boundary, including the immediate basin, has a cusp; see Lemma \ref{lemma:avoid_petals}. Therefore, the same is true for $a_0$ by the local injectivity of $f_1$. Thus, $U_i$ and $U_j$ are not quasidisks, a contradiction. We conclude that the parabolic multiplicity of $a_0$ for $h$ is strictly greater than $2$. 

By Lemma \ref{lemma:avoid_petals} and since $U_i,U_j$ are quasidisks, we see that $f_1(U_i)$ and $f_1(U_j)$ are immediate basins of $b_0$, not necessarily distinct. Note that in a neighborhood of $a_0$ in each of the sets $U_i$ and $U_j$ the map $f_1$ conjugates $h$ to $f_2$. Thus, $U_i,U_j$ contain attracting petals $P_i,P_j$, respectively, of $h$ at $a_0$. In addition, points of $U_i,U_j$ near $a_0$ are absorbed under iteration of $h$ by $P_i,P_j$, respectively. If $nm+1\geq 4$, then $h$ has at least $3$ attracting directions, so there exists a third attracting direction and a corresponding petal $P$  that is disjoint from $U_i$ and $U_j$ and can be taken to be a quasidisk. By assumption, there exists a quasiconformal map of the sphere that sends $U_i$ and $U_j$ to tangent disks. This contradicts Lemma \ref{lemma:room3}.  Therefore, $nm+1 = 3$. This implies that $m = 2$ and $n=1$ or $m=1$ and $n=2$, as required in the two alternatives of Theorem \ref{theorem:uniformization_general} \ref{theorem:uniformization_general:2}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that there exists a quasiconformal map $g$ of $\widehat \mathbb{C}$ that maps each Fatou component of $f$ onto a disk. Condition \ref{r:jordan} is immediate. Each Fatou component is a quasidisk. By Proposition \ref{prop:quasidiskgf} and Remark \ref{remark:prop:quasidisk}, if $f$ has a parabolic periodic point $a_0$, then its multiplicity must be at least $3$. On the other hand, if the multiplicity is strictly greater than $3$, then at least three Fatou components intersect at $a_0$, which is a contradiction. Thus \ref{r:parabolic3} holds. If $a_0$ lies in the boundary of a Fatou component $U$, then $U$ is periodic by Lemma \ref{lemma:no_infinite} \ref{lemma:no_infinite:1} and $U$ is an immediate basin of $a_0$ by Proposition \ref{prop:quasidiskgf}. This establishes condition \ref{r:parabolic_basins} of Theorem \ref{theorem:rational_uniformization}. Finally, suppose that $U,V$ are Fatou components with $\overline{U}\cap \overline{V}\neq \emptyset$. Since the Julia set of $f$ is not a Jordan curve, we have $\partial U\neq \partial V$. Since $g(U)$ and $g(V)$ are tangent disks, $\overline{U}\cap \overline{V}$ must consist of a single point $a_0$. By Theorem \ref{theorem:uniformization_general}, the point $a_0$ is mapped to a parabolic periodic cycle of multiplicity $3$ by an iterate of $f$ that is a local homeomorphism near $a_0$, as required in condition \ref{r:parabolic_tangent} of Theorem \ref{theorem:rational_uniformization}.

    Conversely, suppose that conditions \ref{r:jordan}, \ref{r:parabolic3}, \ref{r:parabolic_basins}, \ref{r:parabolic_tangent} hold and that the Julia set of $f$ is not homeomorphic to $\mathbb S^1$ or $\mathbb S^2$. If there exists only one Fatou component, then this component is a Jordan region by \ref{r:jordan}, so its complement, i.e., the Julia set, has non-empty interior. However, this forces the Julia set to be the entire sphere \cite{Milnor:dynamics}*{Corollary 4.11}, a contradiction. Thus, there exist at least two Fatou components. 
    
    Our goal is to verify the assumptions of Theorem \ref{theorem:uniformization_general} \ref{theorem:uniformization_general:2}. By assumption \ref{r:parabolic3}, there are no parabolic points of multiplicity $2$. Let $U$ be a Fatou component of $f$. By \ref{r:parabolic_basins}, the orbit of $\partial U$ contains the orbit of at most one parabolic periodic point $a$, in which case an immediate basin of $a$ is in the orbit of $U$. Thus, Proposition \ref{prop:quasidiskgf} applies and $U$ is a quasidisk. By condition \ref{r:parabolic_tangent}, if $U,V$ are distinct Fatou components with $\overline{U}\cap \overline{V}\neq \emptyset$, then the intersection $\overline{U}\cap \overline{V}$ consists of a single point $a_0$ that is not critical and it is eventually mapped to a parabolic periodic cycle of multiplicity $3$. Note that $f(U)$ and $f(V)$ are Fatou components that are Jordan regions by \ref{r:jordan}, and they are distinct by Lemma \ref{lemma:no_infinite} \ref{lemma:no_infinite:00}, given that $a_0$ is not a critical point. Applying condition \ref{r:parabolic_tangent} to the pair $f(U),f(V)$, we see that $f(a_0)$ is the unique point in the intersection $\overline{f(U)}\cap \overline{f(V)}$ and $f(a_0)$ is not a critical point. Hence, inductively, the entire forward orbit of $a_0$ is not critical. Hence, $a_0$ is mapped to a parabolic periodic cycle of multiplicity $3$ by an iterate of $f$ that is a local homeomorphism near $a_0$, as in the assumptions of Theorem \ref{theorem:uniformization_general}. 
    
    We now apply Theorem \ref{theorem:uniformization_general}, which implies the existence of a quasiconformal homeomorphism $g\colon \widehat \mathbb{C}\to \widehat \mathbb{C}$ that maps each Fatou component of $f$ onto a disk and is $1$-quasiconformal on the Julia set $J(f)$. Since $J(f)$ has measure zero \cite{McMullen:Hausdorff_GF}*{Corollary 6.2}, the $1$-quasiconformality condition holds vacuously for any such quasiconformal map $g$. By the last part of Theorem \ref{theorem:uniformization_general} we conclude that $g|_{J(f)}$ is unique up to post-composition with M\"obius transformations.

Then the Fatou components of $f$ can be either attracting or parabolic; see the discussion after Theorem 1.5 in \cite{LuoNtalampekos:piecewise_qc}. body_md:
Suppose that $f$ is a unicritical geometrically finite polynomial. If there is no bounded Fatou component, the statement is vacuously true, so we assume that there exists a bounded Fatou component. All bounded periodic Fatou components are either hyperbolic or parabolic. Thus, the unique (finite) critical point of $f$ is contained in the Fatou set and there are no critical points on the Julia set. 
    
    Suppose that there exists a quasiconformal map of $\mathbb{C}$ that maps each bounded Fatou component of $f$ onto a disk. Suppose first that $J(f)$ is not homeomorphic to $\mathbb S^1$.  By Theorem \ref{theorem:polynomial_uniformization}, conditions \ref{r:parabolic3} and \ref{r:parabolic_tangent} hold. Suppose that $f$ has no parabolic points. By \ref{r:parabolic_tangent}, we conclude that bounded Fatou components have disjoint closures. Since there are no critical points on the Julia set, $f$ is hyperbolic \cite{Milnor:dynamics}*{Theorem 19.1}. Now, if $J(f)$ is homeomorphic to $\mathbb S^1$, by Proposition \ref{prop:julia_jordan}, either $f$ has a parabolic periodic point of multiplicity $3$ or $f$ is hyperbolic, as desired. 

    Conversely, suppose that $f$ is hyperbolic and all bounded Fatou components have disjoint closures. If $J(f)$ is homeomorphic to $\mathbb S^1$, then by Proposition \ref{prop:julia_jordan} there exists a quasiconformal map $g$ of $\mathbb{C}$ that maps the bounded Fatou component of $f$ onto a disk. If $J(f)$ is not homeomorphic to $\mathbb S^1$, then conditions \ref{r:parabolic3}, \ref{r:parabolic_basins}, \ref{r:parabolic_tangent} are vacuously true, so by Theorem \ref{theorem:polynomial_uniformization} there exists a quasiconformal map $g$ of $\mathbb{C}$ that maps each bounded Fatou component of $f$ onto a disk. 
    
    Finally, suppose that $f$ has a parabolic periodic point of multiplicity $3$. Since $f$ is unicritical, there is a unique periodic cycle of bounded Fatou components, all of which are immediate basins of this parabolic point; see \cite{Milnor:dynamics}*{Theorem 10.15}. Hence, conditions \ref{r:parabolic3} and \ref{r:parabolic_basins} hold. By Lemma \ref{lem:evenpara} below, condition \ref{r:parabolic_tangent} holds. Thus, by Theorem \ref{theorem:polynomial_uniformization} we conclude that there exists a quasiconformal map $g\colon \mathbb{C}\to \mathbb{C}$ that maps each bounded Fatou component of $f$ to a disk.

label: lem:evenpara
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:evenpara}
    Let $f$ be a unicritical polynomial with a parabolic periodic point of multiplicity at least $3$. Then every contact point between Fatou components is eventually mapped to the parabolic cycle.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $f$ is a geometrically finite polynomial, all bounded Fatou components are Jordan regions \cite{RoeschYin:boundary_fatou}. Let $U,V$ be bounded Fatou components such that $\overline{U}\cap \overline{V}\neq \emptyset$. Since $f$ is a polynomial, the Julia set is the boundary of the basin $\mathcal A(\infty)$, so $\overline{U}\cap \overline{V}$ consists of a single point $a_0$, which is not critical. Since there are no critical points on the Julia set, for each $n\in \mathbb{N}$ the components $f^{\circ n}(U)$ and $f^{\circ n}(V)$ are distinct and touch at $f^{\circ n}(a_0)$; see Lemma \ref{lemma:no_infinite} \ref{lemma:no_infinite:00}. Since $U$ and $V$ are pre-periodic, the point $a_0$ is pre-periodic. Thus, by passing to iterates, it suffices to show that every periodic contact point between two periodic Fatou components is parabolic. 
        
    Let $\{U_1,\dots, U_k\}$ be the collection of bounded periodic Fatou components, and let $\{a_1,\dots, a_l\}$ be the collection of all contact points between $U_i$ and $U_j$, $i\neq j$. We show that $\{a_1,\dots,a_l\}$ is exactly the parabolic cycle. Since $f$ is unicritical, $\{U_1,\dots, U_k\}$ form a single orbit; see \cite{Milnor:dynamics}*{Theorem 10.15}. In particular, $f$ permutes the collection $\{U_1,\dots, U_k\}$ and $f^{\circ k}(U_i)=U_i$ for each $i\in \{1,\dots,k\}$. Moreover, $f$ maps each contact point to a contact point and $f^{\circ k}$ fixes contact points. Therefore $f$ is a bijection on $\{a_1,\dots,a_l\}$.
    
  
    We consider a combinatorial bipartite graph $\Gamma$ with two types of vertices $V_1, V_2$: vertices in $V_1$ are in correspondence with components in $\{U_1,\dots,U_k\}$ and vertices in $V_2$ are in correspondence with contact points $\{a_1,\dots, a_l\}$. A vertex $v\in V_1$ is connected to $w\in V_2$ if the corresponding contact point for $w$ is on the boundary of the component for $v$. By construction, $\Gamma$ is a finite union of trees, and the map $f$ induces a natural graph isomorphism $f_*\colon \Gamma \rightarrow \Gamma$. By the above, $f_*$ is a permutation on $V_1$.

    Let $T$ be a component of $\Gamma$. We claim that $T$ contains exactly one vertex in $V_2$ that corresponds to a point in the parabolic periodic cycle. Indeed, let $A = V_1 \cap T$ and $B = V_2 \cap T$. Since each vertex in $V_2$ has valence at least $2$, every endpoint of $T$ is in $V_1$. Since $f_*$ acts transitively on $V_1$, all vertices of $A$ have the same valence. Thus $A$ is exactly the set of endpoints of $T$. Since $T$ is bipartite, there is a unique vertex $b\in B$ which connects to every vertex in $A$, i.e., $T$ is a star. 
    Since the components corresponding to the vertices of $A$ are parabolic and the parabolic multiplicity is at least $3$, the contact point corresponding to $b$ is parabolic.

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $f(z) = z^d+c$ is hyperbolic, and the closures of any two distinct bounded Fatou components are disjoint. Let $\Omega_1,\dots, \Omega_p$ be the unique cycle of periodic Fatou components of $f$. Then there exist disjoint open sets $V_i$, $i\in \{1,\dots,p\}$, and open sets $U_i$, $i\in \{1,\dots,p\}$ such that $\Omega_i \Subset U_i \Subset V_i$ and the map $f^{\circ p}\colon U_i \to V_i$ is polynomial-like. By the straightening theorem \cite{CarlesonGamelin:Dynamics}*{Theorem VI.1.1}, this polynomial-like map is hybrid equivalent to a unicritical polynomial with an attracting fixed point whose immediate basin contains the critical point. Thus, the corresponding straightening parameter lies in the main hyperbolic component of the Multibrot set. Since the neighborhoods $V_i$, $i\in \{1,\dots,p\}$, are chosen pairwise disjoint, the associated renormalization is primitive. Thus, $c$ is contained in the main hyperbolic component of a primitive Multibrot copy. See \cite{DudkoLyubichMLCFeigenbaum}*{\S 2.2.3--2.2.4} and \cite{MilnorOrbitPortraits}*{\S~6} for the discussion for the Mandelbrot set, and the case for Multibrot set is similar.
        
    Conversely, suppose that $c$ lies in the main hyperbolic component of a primitive Multibrot copy. Then the distinct periodic bounded Fatou components have disjoint closures. We claim that the same is true for all bounded Fatou components. Suppose, to the contrary, that two distinct bounded Fatou components $U, V$ have intersecting closures.
    Since $f$ is hyperbolic, the critical point lies in the Fatou set. Therefore, the images $f^{\circ n}(U), f^{\circ n}(V)$ remain distinct bounded Fatou components whose closures meet at a point (Lemma \ref{lemma:no_infinite} \ref{lemma:no_infinite:00}). Since every bounded Fatou component is eventually periodic, this contradicts the disjointedness of the closures of distinct periodic bounded Fatou components. Hence all bounded Fatou components have pairwise disjoint closures.

    Suppose $f(z) = z^d +c$ has a parabolic periodic point of multiplicity $3$. Let $a$ be a parabolic periodic point with period $p$. Since $f$ is unicritical, $f$ has only one periodic cycle of bounded Fatou components. So the two attracting basins of the parabolic periodic point are contained in the same cycle. Thus, $(f^{\circ p})'(a) = -1$. In the family of unicritical polynomials the multiplier gives a branched covering map of a hyperbolic component to $\mathbb{D}$                                                                              
    \cite{MilnorOrbitPortraits}*{Theorem~6.5 and Remark~6.4}. Thus the period-doubling points correspond to exactly those with multiplier $-1$. Therefore, $c$ is a period-doubling bifurcation point.
    
    Conversely, suppose $c$ is a period-doubling bifurcation point. Then there exists a parabolic periodic point $a$ of period $p$ with $(f^{\circ p})'(a) = -1$. Therefore, there are $2n$ attracting basins at $a$ for some $n\in \mathbb{N}$; see \cite{Milnor:dynamics}*{Lemma 10.4}. Since $f$ is unicritical, there is a unique cycle of attracting basins; see \cite{Milnor:dynamics}*{Theorem 10.15}. Thus, there are exactly two attracting basins at $a$, interchanged by $f^{\circ p}$. In particular, the parabolic multiplicity is $3$.

    We first claim that there exists a continuum $Q \subset \overline{U}$ so that 
    $$
    f(Q) \subset Q \text{ and } Q \cap \partial U = \mathcal{A}.
    $$
    Let $Q_0 \subset \overline{U}$ be a closed attracting petal if $U$ is parabolic or a small forward invariant disk about its attracting fixed point if $U$ is (super-)attracting.  
    Choose arcs $E_x \subset \overline{U}$ landing at the vertices of $x\in \mathcal{A}$ that are dynamically compatible in the sense that 
    \begin{itemize}
        \item if $x$ is the parabolic fixed point, then $E_x \subset Q_0$ and $f(E_x) \subset E_x$ and 
        \item otherwise, $E_{f(x)} \subset f(E_x)$.
    \end{itemize}
    This is possible by considering the Koenigs coordinate at repelling periodic points and taking pull-backs at pre-periodic points. Connect the interior endpoints of these arcs to $Q_0$ by compact arcs in $U$. Let $T$ be their union with $Q_0$. Compatibility near the vertices ensures that $f(T)\setminus T$ is contained in a compact set $C\subset U$. Since $Q_0$ attracts compact subsets of $U$, all sufficiently high forward images of $C$ lie in $Q_0$. Therefore, the set
$$
Q=\overline{\bigcup_{n\ge0}f^{\circ n}(T)}
$$
is a compact forward-invariant continuum and $Q\cap\partial U=\mathcal A$. This completes the proof of the claim.


    Let $X\coloneqq \widehat\mathbb{C} \setminus (Q \cup P(f))$ and $Y \coloneqq \widehat\mathbb{C} \setminus f^{-1}(Q \cup P(f))$. For $\epsilon>0$ and a component $\gamma_i$ of $\partial U\setminus \mathcal A$ we set
    $$
    N_{i, \epsilon} \coloneqq N_{\epsilon, X}(\gamma_i) = \{z\in X:h_X(z,\gamma_i)<\epsilon\}.
    $$
    Recall that $h_X$ denotes the hyperbolic metric on $X$. We claim that for sufficiently small $\epsilon$, $N_{i, \epsilon}$ is contained in some  simply connected domain $H_i \subset X$ such that the domains in $\{H_i\}$ are pairwise disjoint.
    
    Since $Q$ is a non-degenerate continuum through each vertex $v \in \mathcal{A}$, by comparison and Koebe's estimate (see \cite{BeardonMinda:hyperbolic}*{Section 8}), we have
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:estimatenearv}
    \rho_X(z) \geq \rho_{\widehat\mathbb{C}\setminus Q}(z)\gtrsim \frac{1}{|z-v|} \quad \text{for $z\in X$ near $v$.}
    \end{equation}
    We construct $H_i$ as follows. Let $v$ be an endpoint of $\gamma_i$. We first construct two arcs landing at $v$ that locally bound a sector containing $\gamma_i$ such that the $h_X$-distance of the two arcs to $\gamma_i$ is bounded from below. If $v$ is a repelling periodic point, construct the two arcs of $H_i$ in a Koenigs fundamental annulus and iterate them by the inverse return map. By compactness, there is a uniform lower bound for the distance between the two arcs in the metric $|dz|/|z-v|$. So, in view of \eqref{eq:estimatenearv} the distance between each of the two arcs and $\gamma_i$ is bounded from below in the $h_X$-metric. If $v$ is a parabolic fixed point, the existence of the arcs follows from the construction given in \cite{LuoNtalampekos:piecewise_qc}*{Lemma 7.1}; see \cite{LuoNtalampekos:piecewise_qc}*{Figure 7.1}. If $v$ is a strictly pre-periodic point, then the two arcs are constructed by pull-backs. We can connect the arcs at the two endpoints of $\gamma_i$ to obtain a closed curve $\alpha$ which bounds a simply connected domain $H_i \subset X$ and the $h_X$-distance between $\alpha$ and $\gamma_i$ is bounded from below. By choosing disjoint sectors at shared vertices, we may construct the regions $\{H_i\}$ so that they are pairwise disjoint. The claim follows.

    We choose $\epsilon$ sufficiently small so that $N_i\coloneqq N_{i,\epsilon}$ is contained in $H_i$ for each $i$.  Suppose that $f(I_j) = \gamma_i$.  Let $D_j$ be the component of $f^{-1}(N_i)$ that contains $I_j$. Since $H_i$ is simply connected and avoids critical values, the map $f\colon D_j\rightarrow N_i$ is conformal.
    Since the neighborhoods $\{N_i\}$ are pairwise disjoint, the sets $\{D_j\}$ have the same property. Suppose that $I_j \subset \gamma_{k}$. Since $Q \cup P(f)$ is forward invariant, the map $f\colon Y \rightarrow X$ is a covering and the inclusion map $\iota\colon Y \rightarrow X$ is distance-decreasing by the Schwarz--Pick lemma.
    Thus,
    $$
    D_j = N_{\epsilon, Y}(I_j) \subset N_{\epsilon, X}(I_j) \subset N_{\epsilon, X}(\gamma_k) = N_k.
    $$
    This completes the proof.

head: environment
name: Strictly pre-periodic case

title: Proof
body_md:
We adapt the construction given in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:expand}.
    As in Lemma~\ref{lem:expand}, construct a continuum $Q\subset\overline V$ such that
    $$
        f(Q)\subset Q\quad\text{and}\quad Q\cap\partial V=\mathcal A'.
    $$
    We set
    $$
        X=\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus(Q\cup P(f)),\qquad Y=f^{-1}(X),\qquad Z=f^{-2}(X).
    $$
    Forward invariance of $Q$ and $P(f)$ gives that $Z\subset Y$, and that the maps
    $$
        f\colon Y\longrightarrow X,\qquad f^{\circ 2}\colon Z\longrightarrow X
    $$
    are coverings. We equip these surfaces with their hyperbolic metrics. For $\epsilon>0$, let 
    $$
    N_{\epsilon, Y}(\gamma_i) = \{z\in X:h_Y(z,\gamma_i)<\epsilon\}, \quad N_{\epsilon, Z}(I_j) = \{z\in X:h_Z(z,I_j)<\epsilon\}.
    $$
    We claim that for all sufficiently small $\epsilon$, the neighborhood $N_{\epsilon, Y}(\gamma_i)$ (resp.\ $N_{\epsilon, Z}(I_j)$) is contained in a simply connected domain $H_i \subset Y$ (resp.\ $L_j \subset Z$) such that the sets $\{H_i\}$ (resp.\ $\{L_j\}$) are pairwise disjoint. The construction is the same as in Lemma~\ref{lem:expand} away from vertices eventually mapped to parabolic points. If a vertex $b$ is eventually mapped to $a$, let $k$ be the local degree of an iterate taking $b$ to $a$. By hypothesis $k\ge2$. Let $\gamma^\pm$ be the two arcs from the family $\{\gamma_i\}$ with an endpoint $b$. Then $\gamma^\pm$ are separated by a positive angle at $b$, so we can choose local sectors bounded by two arcs with $h_Y$-distance to $\gamma^{\pm}$ bounded from below. Indeed, in suitable local coordinates, $f$ takes the form $z\mapsto z^k$, so the preimage of $V$ near $b$ consists of $k$ components whose closures meet at $b$.
    Since $V$ has a cusp at $a$, the two boundary arcs of each component form an interior angle of $2\pi/k$ at $b$. This proves the claim. 

    Set $N_i=N_{\epsilon,Y}(\gamma_i)$ and $D_j = N_{\epsilon, Z}(I_j)$ for sufficiently small $\epsilon$ so that the previous claim holds. Then the sets $\{N_i\}$ are pairwise disjoint and so are the sets $\{D_j\}$. Suppose that $S(I_j)=\gamma_i$. Since $H_i$ and $L_j$ are simply connected, we may analytically extend $S\colon I_j \rightarrow \gamma_i$ and $T \coloneqq S^{-1}\colon \gamma_i \rightarrow I_j$ to maps
    \begin{align*}
        S\colon L_j\longrightarrow Y\quad \text{such that}\quad  f\circ S=f^{\circ 2}, \\
        T\colon H_i \longrightarrow Z\quad \text{such that} \quad f = f^{\circ 2} \circ T.
    \end{align*}
    By the invariance of the hyperbolic density under the coverings $f$ and $f^{\circ 2}$, we conclude that $S, T$ preserve hyperbolic lengths measured in $Z, Y$. Let $z\in D_j=N_{\epsilon,Z}(I_j)$. Choose a rectifiable path in $Z$ from a point of $I_j$ to $z$ with hyperbolic length less than $\epsilon$. Every point of this path lies in $D_j\subset L_j$, so its image under $S$ starts on $\gamma_i$ and has the same length. Hence $S(z)\in N_i$, proving $S(D_j)\subseteq N_i$. The same argument shows that $T(N_i) \subseteq D_j$. Since $S\circ T, T \circ S$ are identity on $\gamma_i$ and $I_j$ respectively, we conclude that $S(D_j) = N_i$ and the map $S\colon D_j \rightarrow N_i$ is conformal. Finally, if $I_j\subset\gamma_k$, the Schwarz--Pick lemma for the inclusion $Z\subset Y$ gives
    $$
    D_j= N_{\epsilon,Z}(I_j)\subset N_{\epsilon,Y}(I_j) \subset N_{\epsilon,Y}(\gamma_k)=N_k.
    $$
    This completes the proof.

label: proposition:rational_quasidisk
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{proposition:rational_quasidisk}
    Let $f$ be a rational map and suppose that $U$ is a Jordan region, $f(U)$ is a quasidisk, and the map $f\colon U\to f(U)$ is proper. Then $U$ is a quasidisk.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $f(U)$ is a quasidisk, there exists a quasiconformal map $\phi$ of $\widehat \mathbb{C}$ that maps $f(U)$ onto a disk.  By the measurable Riemann mapping theorem \cite{AstalaIwaniecMartin:quasiconformal}*{Theorem 5.3.4}, there exists a quasiconformal map $\psi$ of $\widehat \mathbb{C}$ whose Beltrami coefficient is the same as that of $\phi\circ f$. Then the map $\phi\circ f\circ \psi^{-1}$ is rational (see \cite{AstalaIwaniecMartin:quasiconformal}*{Theorem 5.5.1}) and maps the Jordan region $\psi(U)$ onto a disk. 

    Therefore, by Theorem \ref{theorem:quasidisk_quasicircle}, it suffices to prove that if $g$ is a rational map and $J$ is a Jordan curve that is mapped onto a circle, then $J$ is a quasicircle. For this, it suffices to prove that the Ahlfors condition \eqref{condition:ahlfors} holds near critical points of $g$ on $J$. By precomposing $g$ with a conformal map near a critical point $z_0\in J$ and post-composing with a M\"obius transformation, we may assume that $g(z)=(z-z_0)^d$ in a neighborhood of $z_0$ for some $d\geq 2$ and $g$ maps an arc $A$ of $J$ that passes through $z_0$ onto a line segment passing through $0$. We observe that $A$ is the union of two non-overlapping segments with a common endpoint at $0$. Thus, the Ahlfors condition holds trivially on the arc $A$.
